articles.title: USAF should buy newly designed air refuelers to meet China threat: Report
articles.snippet: Although there’s a “temptation” to keep buying KC-46s, a plan to procure 75 more of the Boeing-made tankers should be an “upper limit” followed by a new, longer range tanker, the Hudson Institute’s Timothy Walton told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Air Force requires a slew of investments to shore up its air refueling fleet, from targeted infrastructure spending to designing a new tanker with greater range and fuel offload capacity, according to a think tank report.
Published today, the report by Hudson Institute experts Timothy Walton and Shane Dennin — titled Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations — offers a comprehensive view of the Air Force’s air refueling capacity. The service currently relies on “vulnerable forward bases” and tankers with insufficient range, increasing the risk of defeat in a direct conflict with China, the report says.
Among its findings, the report notes that the Boeing-built KC-46 Pegasus — which is slowly replacing the Air Force’s Eisenhower-era KC-135 Stratotanker — “lacks the range, offload and survivability” to prevail in a conflict with Beijing. To retain the Air Force’s aerial refueling advantage, the report recommends three key steps for future tanker planning:
- Develop and field a medium-sized tanker with greater range and fuel capacity, such as a blended-wing body (BWB) aircraft. Assuming a fleet of 510 tankers, acquiring 260 KC-46s and 250 BWB refuelers could cost an estimated $397.6 billion across R&D, procurement and sustainment — about $15.5 billion less than simply buying only the same number of Pegasus aircraft, according to the report.
- Strengthen airfield resilience with infrastructure investments and improved defenses, along with steps like adopting greater distributed fuel storage. The authors estimate these measures could cumulatively cost approximately $35.5 billion.
- Equip tankers with new mission systems to boost connectivity, improve operations and aid self-defense. The report estimates these upgrades
Following what military officials have described as the platform’s success in recent combat operations like Epic Fury, “[t]here’s a temptation for the Air Force to continue buying KC-46s,” Walton told Breaking Defense in an interview ahead of the report’s release. Still, “there’s clearly a need for a new approach that goes beyond what the KC-46 provides.”
An Air Force spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the service is investing in tanker capacity, improving the KC-46 and developing next-generation refueling capabilities while pursuing follow-on solutions to address fleet survivability.
Boeing did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Air Force last year unveiled plans to order up to 75 additional KC-46s while the service studies options for a next-gen tanker. Walton reasoned that 75 aircraft “should be the upper limit of that buy” and argued that the service should prioritize developing a new tanker. Depending on future budget constraints, that approach could require trade-offs such as trimming KC-46 procurement.
The report outlines five different approaches to the Air Force’s tanker fleet, ranging from purchasing only Pegasus aircraft to fielding a mix of KC-46s, KC-135s and specialized, low-observable refuelers designed to offload fuel closer to the fight. Though each approach has its own strengths, Walton highlighted fielding a medium-sized BWB aircraft as a desirable and “fiscally achievable plan” — adding that such an aircraft could enter service around 2032.
The Air Force is funding a BWB demonstrator aircraft designed by startup JetZero, which military officials have described as a potential candidate for future mobility missions. Walton said the report used a “representative” BWB model, and that while JetZero’s aircraft may fit the bill, other vendors could offer viable designs.
RELATED: Natilus secures Air Force contract to develop blended wing body aircraft
Iranian strikes that have destroyed US aircraft on the ground also underscore the need for more resilient base infrastructure, including hardened fuel storage and aircraft shelters, Walton said. Top military brass have championed passive and active defenses at airfields, but not everyone agrees with measures to build more hardened aircraft shelters, including Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach.
“It’s probably most contentious to assert that tanker aircraft should also be under consideration for hardened aircraft shelters, or at least hangars that can cover them from observation,” Walton said. “But I think in light of what we’ve seen from Operation Epic Fury, it’s necessary.”
Walton argued that the Air Force could fund more resilient infrastructure through existing plans to increase spending on facilities, especially if those funding levels are sustained. As large aircraft that serve a critical need, refueling assets are often seen as high-priority targets, though Walton noted that hardened shelters have generally been built for fighters.
“It’s not necessarily more money, but it’s prioritizing the amount of money in the out-years,” he said.
The Air Force is incrementally equipping its mobility aircraft with modern communications equipment and exploring self-defense systems that could defeat enemy attacks. But the service has previously failed to meet ambitious targets for fleet connectivity, and Walton acknowledged that limited resources could constrain the report’s recommendations for new mission systems, including communications, self-defense and autonomy technologies.
“Moving forward, the Air Force will have to weigh its available budget to spend” on new mission systems alongside competing priorities, he said, like resilient infrastructure and fielding a clean-sheet tanker. “And that might lead to some hard decisions.”

articles.title: Is the Pentagon’s demand signal for drones working? It depends on who you ask.
articles.snippet: “There’s a lot of positive signaling, but we need to see the whites of the eyes: We need to see sustained, normalized demand,” said James Slider, CEO of Performance Drone Works.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — As the Pentagon rushes to ramp up aerial drone production, industry and military officials tell Breaking Defense they are divided over whether the department’s approach can generate the sustained demand needed to build a lasting domestic drone industry.
“There’s a lot of positive signaling, but we need to see the whites of the eyes: We need to see sustained, normalized demand,” James Slider, CEO of Performance Drone Works, recently told Breaking Defense.
“So what does that look like?” Slider added. “If you win an award and then you’re providing 1,000 drones a month for a year, that’s a very healthy demand for us.”
The Pentagon has created multiple funding avenues and acquisition competitions to encourage companies to develop drones and expand production, without necessarily guaranteeing the longer-term orders needed to justify those investments. The strategy is intended to build up domestic manufacturing capacity, but industry leaders say uncertainty over future purchases could undermine that goal.
As the largest single source of demand for small drones, the Army is deliberately trying to push companies to invest in domestic production, even as some manufacturers question whether that demand will be enough to sustain their businesses.
Jon Strzelec, advanced manufacturing lead for small drones at Army Materiel Command, said the military recognizes that companies are reluctant to invest without more certainty about future orders. Therefore, the department is trying to “artificially induce” demand signals for industry at large.
“We’re trying to force a supply chain to stand up within the country, and so there’s a lot of companies that say, there’s just not enough demand for me to invest in that,” he recently told Breaking Defense.
Whether that signal can be boosted strongly enough to convince cautious industry officials may determine the fate of the Pentagon’s drone push — and billions of dollars in proposed defense spending.
An ‘Artificial’ Push
The push to acquire small, cheap aerial drones is not brand new. Under the Biden administration, the Pentagon launched its Replicator initiative to rapidly acquire and field thousands of inexpensive, attritable drones to prepare for a potential military contingency with China.
Over the past year and a half, however, that effort has accelerated. The Pentagon is now pursuing new acquisition programs, reorganizing how it manages autonomous warfare initiatives and seeking billions of dollars for drone purchases.
In mid-2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth kicked off the broader push when he issued the Drone Dominance memo, laying out plans to boost unmanned aerial systems production, cut red tape associated with troops’ use of those aerial weapons, and equip every Army squad with small, one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026.
The Pentagon has since reshuffled its autonomy leadership, with Hegseth seeking congressional approval for a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM. Meanwhile, the Biden-era Replicator initiative was repackaged as the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG) and later absorbed into Task Force Autonomous Warfare.
The Pentagon has outlined plans to spend nearly $55 billion on the initiative in its FY27 budget. But the bulk of that funding was requested through a reconciliation package, leaving its future uncertain as lawmakers weigh whether to approve the money and the department considers whether to retool its base budget request.
One of the clearest examples of the department’s approach is its Drone Dominance program, a gauntlet-style competition billed as a way to give companies repeated opportunities to win smaller deals that will collectively amount to $1 billion over two years. An online leaderboard tracks competitors in each gauntlet, including the number of drones ordered and each company’s reported delivery status.
“They’re artificially creating a demand signal to push the American industry to start manufacturing this stuff in the United States,” Strzelec said.
Under Gauntlet 1, the Pentagon has selected 11 companies to deliver 30,000 small drones through a combination of initial and “bonus” orders. At the lower end of the ordering scale, the department ordered 1,520 drones from Farage Precision while toward the top, Neros has received orders for 4,960.
For Gauntlet 2, the department divided drones into two categories — those best suited for deep strike and those better aligned for close-quarters combat. It has tapped five companies in both categories and awarded deals covering 30,000 drones in each.
But Drone Dominance awards do not guarantee future orders, leaving companies without a commitment to sustain production beyond their initial contracts.
That uncertainty reflects a broader challenge in the Pentagon’s acquisition strategy, as repeated competitions can give the military opportunities to select new technologies and encourage companies to improve their systems. But without predictable follow-on orders, the same approach can make it harder for manufacturers to justify long-term investments needed to scale — a conflict not lost on defense officials.
Andrew Evans, director of the Strategy & Transformation Office inside the Army’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence (G-2), called it an “ultimate economic challenge” for the department as it tries to leverage existing American manufacturing capacity while ensuring production lines remain open even when demand falls.
“The challenge that our senior leaders are having to contend with is, how do you incentivize industry to build if your ordering period is so episodic?” he said during a recent interview with Breaking Defense.
Strategic Gamble
Whether companies are buying into the demand signal the Pentagon is hoping to provide remains up in the air, according to multiple interviews and comments made this month from industry leaders. Some described strong demand across government, while others questioned whether that demand would translate into sustained orders.
In an interview with Breaking Defense on Oct. 13, Skydio Chief Revenue Officer Callan Carpenter said that from his perspective, the administration’s demand signal to industry is clear.
“The demand signals are very strong, and it’s not just DOW [the Department of War] either,” Carpenter said, referring to the Trump administration’s alternate name for the Defense Department. “It’s [Department of Homeland Security], it’s other parts of the civilian federal government, and we’re selling products into all of those segments,”
Other industry leaders offered differing opinions, noting challenges with smaller buys, a never-ending cycle of competitions and annual funds that are not yet approved by Congress or reflected in projected outyear spending requests.
John Burer, CEO for the American Center for Manufacturing & Innovation industry group, explained that companies need confidence that they will win contracts and produce drones at scale before committing to major capital expenditures.
“If I were a manufacturer of drone systems, I wouldn’t be investing ahead of a very large amount of money or a consistent demand signal,” he told Breaking Defense. “It’s great to do a bake off and to test some of these things and prove out that they can work, but then scaling production needs a different mindset, and it’s a cost focus oftentimes.”
Chad Chasteen, senior director and team leader of Army business development at AV, said that while the service’s preference for frequently running competitions affords more opportunities for companies to win a contract, the approach also comes with drawbacks.
“The Army system of continuous competition and not sticking with a solution for more than a year or two creates all kinds of havoc in the supply chain,” he said Oct. 13 during a panel at the AUSA conference. He added that successive competitions also need to be followed by a similar number of awards.
“There is no supply without demand,” he said. “Continuous competition doesn’t mean you make industry fill out continuous requests for white papers. There has to be continuous awards, continuous orders to create that.”
Performance Drone Works’ Slider voiced similar concerns about the Pentagon’s long-term demand signal, saying he did not expect much more private equity flow into the sector without stronger commitments.
For Slider, part of the uncertainty stems from the proposed $55 billion DAWG funding package, which remains stalled in Congress. However, if Pentagon leaders and lawmakers find a way to fund the initiative at those levels, even in a base request, that would be a big green flag.
“Seeing the DAWG money flow down would be very encouraging for us,” Slider said. “Depending on who you talk to, it’s definitely coming or definitely not coming.”
Michael Marrow contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: Hackers repeatedly breached suppliers holding UK police data, watchdog finds
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services says British police data has been breach several times this decade through third-party IT suppliers.
articles.full_text:
Hackers repeatedly breached suppliers holding UK police data, watchdog finds
Hackers have repeatedly compromised third-party suppliers holding British police data since 2021, according to a report published Tuesday by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services.
The inspectorate, which oversees policing in England and Wales and fire services in England, said the Police Digital Service and the National Police Chiefs’ Council shared “information on multiple cyberattacks” affecting “third-party ICT supply chains which held police information.”
The report does not say how many attacks took place, which suppliers or forces were affected, or whether data was stolen in these supply-chain incidents. The inspectorate said it purposefully removed operational details that it considered unsuitable for the public domain.
Neither the Home Office, Britain’s interior ministry, nor the National Police Chiefs’ Council responded to questions about whether police data was compromised in the supplier attacks.
The watchdog said the Police Digital Service recorded 252 cybersecurity incidents affecting policing in the first three months of this year, as well as 796 “near misses,” which the report defined as incidents with no harmful breach of data or IT systems.
The report does not say how many of the 252 incidents involved data loss, nor does it break the figure down beyond saying the incidents included malware attacks, unauthorized access attempts and accidental disclosures by police staff.
Elsewhere in the report, the inspectorate said it identified “examples of police forces and fire and rescue services experiencing cyberattacks,” describing incidents that hit operational systems, compromised data and disrupted services.
Leaders in both sectors told the watchdog that “further attacks were highly likely.”
Vague insights about suppliers
The Police Digital Service, set up by the British government in 2021, runs a national security operations center that monitors cyberthreats across policing. It warned the watchdog that police data held on suppliers’ systems was among the biggest risks the sector faces because of how that data sits outside its monitoring.
According to the report, the risk is particularly critical where suppliers handle information on victims, safeguarding, intelligence and investigations.
Inspectors found that most police supplier contracts included no ongoing cybersecurity assurance. In some cases, staff could not say whether suppliers were obliged to report incidents promptly, and in several organizations the system logs held by suppliers were not routinely visible to in-house teams.
The inspectorate also criticized the government for leaving policing and fire services out of the National Risk Register 2025, the Government Cyber Action Plan published in January and the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is still going through Parliament.
Inspectors said no government official they asked could explain why the two sectors were left out of the action plan or the bill. The report called the omission concerning, given the vital role both sectors play in public safety.
Although the report does not provide detail on the breaches it counts, some incidents that took place during the timeframe given are public. In 2023, a ransomware attack on ID card maker Digital ID exposed the details of Metropolitan Police officers and staff and led to the theft of thousands of Greater Manchester Police officers’ names and photos.
In July, the Police National Legal Database, a reference service run by West Yorkshire Police and used by every force in England and Wales, confirmed that hackers had stolen the contact details of officers and staff. The service said its database held no confidential information about victims, witnesses or offenders.
Dyfed-Powys Police in Wales disclosed in September that a cyberattack disrupted some of the force’s non-emergency systems and may have compromised staff information.
Abroad, Dutch police blamed a likely state actor for a 2024 breach of officers’ contact details. In the U.S., the FBI said this year that hackers gained access through a third party to a network holding wiretap data, an intrusion investigators reportedly suspect was carried out by China.
“The cyber threat to police forces and fire and rescue services is significant and expanding rapidly,” said Michelle Skeer, His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary. “A major cyberattack is not a hypothetical scenario.”
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: University of New Mexico hospital diverts ambulances after cyberattack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: For about two hours on Monday, the organization diverted ambulances to health systems in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. They were forced to suspend outpatient surgeries and appointments for the remainder of the day.
articles.full_text:
University of New Mexico hospital diverts ambulances after cyberattack
Ambulances were diverted from the University of New Mexico Health System after a cyberattack caused significant issues for the organization on Monday.
The organization said it suffered a cyberattack on Monday that forced the organization’s IT team to contain the issue and notify federal law enforcement.
For about two hours on Monday, the organization diverted ambulances to health systems in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. They were forced to suspend outpatient surgeries and appointments for the remainder of the day.
“The cybersecurity threat is affecting the entire University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center,” a spokesperson explained. The Health System is one part of the overarching Sciences Center, which also includes an academic campus and medical research facilities.
The health system has the state’s only burn unit, children’s hospital and Level 1 trauma center, and serves a large percentage of the state’s uninsured population.
Local news outlets reported that employees got an alert on their phones notifying them of the cyberattack and instructing them to turn off and unplug all desktops. Employees were asked to disconnect all mobile devices from the hospital Wi-Fi.
Late in the afternoon on Monday, the University of New Mexico Health System began resuming operations and bringing systems back online. Patients who had appointments or procedures cancelled on Monday will be rescheduled, a spokesperson said.
In an updated statement late on Monday, a spokesperson said all appointments will resume as scheduled on Tuesday but classes at the School of Medicine, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy and College of Population Health are canceled on Tuesday. This includes online and remote classes.
UNM Health Sciences academic and research units will also remain closed on Tuesday. Nonessential employees at the UNM Health Sciences Center were asked to remain home on Tuesday.
“We recognize this event may have impacted patients, employees and students, and we appreciate their patience as our teams respond,” the spokesperson said. “Because this remains an active law enforcement investigation, we are limited in what we can share at this time.”
The spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment about whether the incident involved ransomware.
A ransomware gang known as BYOD took credit for the attack on Monday evening, claiming to have compromised 36,000 machines on the university’s main campus and hospital. The cybercriminals said they stole information on students, patients and employees of the organization.
BYOD is a new ransomware gang that emerged last month and little is known about the group, with only a handful of named victims.
This is the second major cyberattack on a large state hospital this year after hackers shut down the University of Mississippi Medical Center in March. That ransomware attack caused chaos in the state for weeks and severely limited operations at the state’s only children's hospital and only Level I trauma center.
Ransomware gangs have repeatedly targeted public services in recent days, taking down dozens of systems run by the city of Columbia, South Carolina last week. City Manager Teresa Wilson confirmed on Friday that they are dealing with a ransomware attack and said several resident-facing systems continued to be knocked offline due to the incident.

is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Malicious apps prey on Russians’ anxiety about fuel prices, drone strikes
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Cybercriminals are stuffing infostealer malware into bogus apps aimed at tracking gas prices, police activity, drone strikes and other information of concern to average Russians, researchers said.
articles.full_text:
Malicious apps prey on Russians’ anxiety about fuel prices, drone strikes
Cybercriminals are exploiting fuel shortages and fears of drone attacks in Russia to trick users into downloading malicious Android apps designed to steal personal and financial information, according to a new report.
The latest campaign targets Russian drivers with an app that claims to show the locations of traffic police patrols, speed cameras and gas stations with fuel in stock. Instead, it delivers ZloyRAT, an Android trojan capable of collecting sensitive information and accessing functions on infected phones, according to researchers at Russian cybersecurity firm F6.
The malware is also being distributed through two other fake applications: GosuVPN, advertised as a free government-backed service for accessing the unrestricted internet, and Drone Radar, which claims to display drone attacks on an interactive map in real time.
All three apps are promoted through a website registered in early October, researchers said, adding that they had requested to block the website in Russia.
The campaign comes as Russia faces widespread fuel shortages and rising gasoline prices, driven in part by repeated long-range Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on Russian oil refineries. The threat actor behind the campaign also remains unknown
F6 said malicious applications targeting drivers are typically advertised in online communities for truck drivers, taxi operators and delivery workers.
Info-stealing malware
ZloyRAT was first identified by F6 earlier this year.
Once installed, it disguises itself as a legitimate app and requests permission to access text messages, contacts and phone calls. It can collect incoming text messages and push notifications, send messages and make calls from an infected device.
The trojan also targets information associated with more than 60 Russian banking and financial apps, as well as online marketplaces, government services and the Telegram messaging platform.
To conceal its activity, ZloyRAT can display a legitimate website when users interact with the malicious app, making it harder for them to recognize that their device has been compromised. Researchers said infected phones may also experience slower performance.
F6 did not disclose how many people had downloaded the apps or whether the campaign had resulted in confirmed financial losses.
A growing market for scams
The campaign is part of a broader wave of cybercrime exploiting Russia's wartime disruptions, particularly concerns about drone strikes and fuel availability.
Earlier this year, F6 identified another Android app, called RadarTrevog, that masqueraded as a drone warning service while distributing RedWing Stealer, a type of malware designed to steal information from infected devices. Researchers discovered more than 800 samples of the malware hidden in apps advertised as drone alert services, fuel availability maps, VPNs and other mobile tools.
Fuel shortages have also created opportunities for online fraud.
In the fall, scammers set up at least 17 websites under the FuelDrive brand, advertising bulk fuel deliveries across Russia. Another operation, uncovered in August, used a fictitious company called Toplivo24 to offer gasoline, diesel and natural gas at prices up to 30 percent below market rates.
In July, F6 identified more than 60 fraudulent websites, some posing as gas station maps, designed to hijack Telegram accounts. A separate campaign offered drivers the chance to reserve 20 liters of gasoline in advance, supposedly allowing them to avoid fuel shortages and long lines.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Moscow faces internet disruptions as foreign leaders gather for summits
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The restrictions will be in place from October 27 to 29, coinciding with the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit and the Russia-Africa summit, Russia's Ministry of Digital Development said Monday.
articles.full_text:
Moscow faces internet disruptions as foreign leaders gather for summits
Russia warned that mobile internet access in central Moscow could be disrupted this week as authorities tighten security ahead of two international summits expected to draw foreign leaders to the capital.
The restrictions will be in place from October 27 to 29, coinciding with the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit and the Russia-Africa summit, Russia's Ministry of Digital Development said Monday.
Voice calls, Wi-Fi networks and websites on a government-approved list will remain accessible during the disruptions, the ministry said.
The list, known as the internet "whitelist," includes government websites, Russian social media platforms, banks and online marketplaces. Introduced in 2025 amid widespread mobile internet shutdowns, the system allows users to access selected services while much of the wider internet remains unavailable.
The restrictions come as Moscow prepares to host senior officials from several countries, including the presidents of Iran and Equatorial Guinea, the emir of Qatar, the chairman of Libya's Presidential Council and Venezuela's vice president, who are expected to attend the gas exporters' summit.
Representatives from around 50 African countries are also expected to attend the Russia-Africa summit. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said President Vladimir Putin planned to hold about 20 bilateral meetings with visiting leaders.
Mobile internet shutdowns have become increasingly common across Russia since spring 2025, with authorities citing the threat of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Moscow has experienced similar restrictions during major political events. In May 2025, authorities restricted mobile internet access in the capital and surrounding regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations attended by several foreign leaders. In March 2026, mobile internet service in central Moscow was disrupted for nearly a week, with officials citing security concerns.
Russian internet freedom advocates have questioned the effectiveness of such measures, arguing that drones do not necessarily rely on mobile internet connections to operate. They have suggested that some regional officials may impose sweeping restrictions to demonstrate to the Kremlin that they are taking action against drone threats.
Rights groups say the shutdowns are part of a broader tightening of internet controls since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
According to Human Rights Watch, Russian authorities have blocked thousands of websites, slowed access to YouTube, removed virtual private network (VPN) apps from app stores and banned major Western social media platforms, including Facebook and Instagram.
Russian authorities have also restricted communications and access to social media during protests, elections and other politically sensitive events.

articles.title: CISA warns of PHP bug exploitation attempts, gives federal agencies days to patch
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: CISA added the widely publicized PHP vulnerabilities to the KEV, but didn't specify what kind of exploitation it was observing.
articles.full_text:
CISA warns of PHP bug exploitation attempts, gives federal agencies days to patch
The federal cybersecurity agency confirmed that two PHP vulnerabilities are being targeted, and ordered all civilian agencies to patch them by Thursday.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the bugs to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Monday evening but declined to answer questions about the nature of the exploitation or potential victims. Within the federal government itself, it’s unclear how many systems might use PHP.
The vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — caused global alarm last Tuesday due to the ubiquity of the PHP programming language across the internet. But throughout the week and into the weekend, experts tempered concerns of mass exploitation due to the lack of viable proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits.
A spokesperson for the agency directed Recorded Future News to a section of the KEV rules that said CISA considers “active exploitation” to include both attempted and successful exploitation of vulnerabilities.
Both Sophos and Palo Alto Networks have in recent days posted and then retracted claims of successful exploitation but several experts were able to discover ways to exploit the bugs by Sunday.
In an updated advisory about the vulnerabilities, CISA urged organizations to identify and inventory systems running any version of PHP, apply the patch or take PHP-based systems offline if they cannot be updated immediately.
In some cases, web application firewalls may provide some level of protection for a period of time, CISA added.
The advisory links to guidance from PHP as well as government cybersecurity agencies in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and others.
Despite the lack of confirmed successful exploitation, dozens of cybersecurity and tech companies reported thousands of failed attempts to use the bugs in attacks.
PHP is used to build and run web applications and the vast majority of websites. Some estimates show that more than 70% of all websites on the internet use PHP. Dozens of governments and businesses took their websites offline last week in an effort to address the vulnerabilities.
Experts have expressed deep concern that millions of PHP-backed websites are still running ancient versions of the language that likely cannot be updated.
Censys created a PHP2Shell dashboard that says of the 42 million Internet-facing PHP services, more than 10 million have been patched since October 21.

is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”
